prompt.context: Our client, Vitality Insurance, is a leading provider of supplemental insurance products in the United States. Vitality agents partner with companies to offer their employees optional, supplemental insurance for such conditions as life, cancer, etc. Vitality has undergone fairly steady growth in the past two years, but they suspect that some of their costs may be out of whack.
prompt.question: Is it true that Vitality's costs are out of whack, and if so, what should they do about it?

clarifying_info.q: How does Vitality sell its products?
clarifying_info.a: Vitality sells all policies through its field sales agents, who are solely compensated on a percentage commission of total new premium, defined as premium from new customers or additional premium (up-sell) from existing policyholders.

clarifying_info.q: How does Vitality communicate short-term priorities to agents?
clarifying_info.a: In addition to the base commission, short-term priorities are often communicated via sales contests that focus on a particular customer segment or activity.

clarifying_info.q: How large is Vitality's sales force?
clarifying_info.a: Vitality is the leader in its category and has over 10,000 field sales agents.

clarifying_info.q: What are the major cost categories?
clarifying_info.a: Major costs are sales, G&A, and advertising.

clarifying_info.q: What is the competitive environment like?
clarifying_info.a: Vitality has a few competitors who have seen similar growth, but Vitality is the leader and competition is not the focus of this case.
It is a mature market. Agent turnover is very high on a yearly basis, though it was lower during the recessionary period.

exhibits.title: Vitality Insurance Key Results and Costs
exhibits.shows: A table of Vitality's key operating metrics and cost line items for 2008, 2009, and 2010 (figures in $000s).

exhibits.title: Vitality Insurance Sales Process — Contest Mix
exhibits.shows: A table showing the number of agent-focused sales contests targeted at each leverage point in the selling process (Hire new agents, Acquire new accounts, Gain active policyholders, Keep accounts active, Produce results/Premium, Reactivating dormant account) for 2008, 2009, and 2010.

exhibits.title: Snapshot of 'Sweeps Week' Contest Results
exhibits.shows: A line chart of actual weekly premium as a percent of historical average premium (2008-2010) for weeks 1-27 (Jan-Jun), with lines for 2008, 2009, and 2010. Two weeks in 2010 are labeled as 'Sweeps Week (1)' and 'Sweeps Week (2)'.
exhibits.data: Y-axis: 0%-200% of historical average. X-axis: weeks 1-27. In 2010, weeks 4 and 20 spike to ~200% (Sweeps Week 1 and 2), while weeks immediately before and after those spikes dip significantly below average. 2008 and 2009 lines remain relatively flat near 100% throughout.

framework: 1. Diagnose which cost line is out of whack by reviewing Exhibit 1 (all costs vs. premium growth)
2. Isolate the anomalous cost: identify that sales costs grew ~45% from 2009 to 2010 while premium grew only 10%
3. Investigate the root cause by examining the sales process and contest structure (Exhibit 2)
4. Identify the specific contest — 'Sweeps Week' — that drove the cost spike and evaluate its effectiveness using Exhibit 3
5. Assess whether the incremental revenue generated by the contest justifies the additional cost
6. Recommend action: eliminate or restructure the ineffective contest and redirect funds

questions.prompt: Looking at Exhibit 1, what do you notice about Vitality's costs relative to revenue growth?
questions.guidance: A strong candidate should quickly notice that accounts converted, policyholders enrolled, and total premium all grow at ~10% per year (consistent with G&A and advertising). However, sales costs grow from $250K to $275K (10%) from 2008 to 2009, but then jump from $275K to $400K (~45%) from 2009 to 2010 — far outpacing 10% premium growth. Profit margin declines from 9.4% to 8.5%, confirming the cost increase is not paying off in revenue.

math.setup: Calculate year-over-year growth rates for sales costs and compare to premium growth
steps: Excess sales cost in 2010 vs. expected at 10% growth: $275K * 1.10 = $302.5K; Actual = $400K; Excess = $97.5K
math.answer: Sales costs grew ~45% while revenue grew only 10% in 2010, creating approximately $97.5K in excess sales spend. Profit margin fell from 9.4% to 8.5%.

questions.prompt: Looking at Exhibit 2, what changed in Vitality's sales contest structure in 2010?
questions.guidance: The contest mix shifted significantly in 2010. Contests aimed at 'Gain active policyholders' dropped from 4 to 0, while contests focused on 'Acquire new accounts' doubled from 2 to 4, and contests on 'Produce results (Premium)' doubled from 2 to 4. This means in 2010 Vitality focused much more on generating new premium and new accounts, and much less on retaining/activating existing policyholders. The candidate should note this shift and ask about the specific new contests — particularly the premium-focused ones — since new customer acquisition is more expensive than retaining existing customers.

questions.prompt: What was the 'Sweeps Week' contest and what does Exhibit 3 tell you about its effectiveness?
questions.guidance: 'Sweeps Week' was a contest launched in 2010 that paid an extra 10% commission on all premium booked during two traditionally low-volume weeks (weeks 4 and 20). Exhibit 3 shows that in those two weeks, premium spiked to ~200% of historical average. However, the weeks immediately surrounding the Sweeps Weeks dipped well below average. This pattern strongly suggests agents were 'gaming' the system by shifting/pulling sales into the contest weeks to earn the extra commission — not generating truly incremental new business. The contest duplicated the incentive already embedded in the base commission (both reward premium volume), so it added cost without creating new value.

math.setup: Estimate the extra cost of Sweeps Week: Vitality paid an extra 10% commission on premium booked in those two weeks
steps: Assume Sweeps Week premium is roughly 2x average weekly premium. 2010 annual premium ≈ $3,025,000K; 52 weeks → avg weekly ≈ $58,173K per week
Extra premium in Sweeps Week (2 weeks, ~2x normal): incremental premium ≈ $58,173K per week × 2 weeks = $116,346K in premium; but much of this is shifted, not new
Extra 10% commission on all Sweeps Week premium (2 weeks at ~2x): 10% × ($58,173K × 2 × 2) ≈ $23,269K additional cost
This is an approximate illustration; the case does not provide exact sweeps week premium figures
math.answer: Sweeps Week created a spike in weekly premium but at significant extra commission cost, and the surrounding-week dips suggest the business was merely shifted — not genuinely incremental. The contest was ineffective and added costs without corresponding profit.

brainstorming.prompt: What should Vitality do to improve its sales cost structure and sales contest strategy going forward?

categories.name: Eliminate ineffective contests
ideas: Eliminate 'Sweeps Week' for 2011 since it duplicates the main commission incentive and merely shifts sales timing
Audit all 2010 contests to identify which are redundant with the base commission structure

categories.name: Repurpose contest budget
ideas: Redirect 'Sweeps Week' budget toward contests that address activities NOT covered by the main commission (e.g., customer retention, reactivating dormant accounts)
Design contests with metrics that are genuinely incremental and additive to base commission incentives

categories.name: New accounts contest caution
ideas: Carefully evaluate whether to eliminate increased new-account contests — the shift may reflect a deliberate new-customer growth strategy
Note that acquiring new customers is more expensive than retaining existing ones, so increased new-account focus likely also hurts margins
If new-account growth is a strategic priority, ensure the economics justify the extra acquisition cost

categories.name: Monitoring and governance
ideas: Implement guardrails that prevent agents from manipulating enrollment timing (currently agents can shift bookings by up to one week)
Track weekly premium trends in real time to detect gaming behavior early
Establish a contest review process to evaluate ROI before launch

categories.name: Retention and upsell focus
ideas: Rebalance contest mix back toward retaining existing policyholders and up-selling, which carry lower cost-to-serve
Consider contests that reward multi-year policyholder retention or cross-sell attach rates

recommendation: Eliminate 'Sweeps Week' for 2011: the contest duplicated the base commission incentive, incentivized agents to game enrollment timing rather than create new business, and materially increased sales costs (~$97.5K excess spend) without a corresponding increase in premium growth or profit margin

Repurpose the freed-up contest budget toward activities not already rewarded by the main commission structure — such as retaining active policyholders, reactivating dormant accounts, or cross-selling — to drive genuinely incremental value
Conduct a broader audit of the 2010 contest mix, particularly the four new-account contests, before deciding whether to maintain or reduce them
risks: Sales force morale: eliminating a popular contest ('Sweeps Week' was well-liked by agents) could dampen motivation if not replaced with an equally engaging alternative
New account growth: if the increased new-account contests reflect a deliberate strategic push, removing them could slow customer acquisition
Gaming recurrence: without tighter timing controls, agents may find other ways to shift business around future contests
next_steps: Quantify the true net-new premium generated by Sweeps Week (strip out shifted business) to confirm the ROI is negative
Engage the sales leadership team to design replacement contests that target behaviors genuinely uncovered by the commission structure
Implement a contest governance process: pre-launch ROI modeling and post-contest audit
Consider whether high agent turnover warrants any changes to the base commission structure to improve retention
